title: Seven Cards, Small Hand
statement:
Cards numbered $1, 2, \dots, 7$ are shuffled so that all $7!$ orderings are equally likely, and are then drawn one at a time in that order. Each drawn card goes into the player's hand. After each draw, the following rule is applied for as long as possible: if the hand contains the smallest-numbered card that has not yet been played, that card is played, which removes it from the hand. The player loses if, after this rule has been applied following some draw, the hand holds $3$ cards.

The probability that the player does not lose is $\frac{m}{n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are coprime positive integers. Find $m + n$.
hints: Look at where card $1$ sits in the ordering. No card can be played until card $1$ has been drawn, so what happens to the hand if card $1$ arrives late?

Card $1$ must be among the first three cards drawn. Set up a recursion on the number of cards: delete card $1$ from the ordering and compare the original game with the game played on the remaining cards.

Let $S(k)$ be the number of orderings of $k$ cards on which the player does not lose. If card $1$ is among the first three cards, deleting it leaves an ordering that is safe exactly when the original was safe, since from the draw of card $1$ onwards the two games have the same hand. This gives $S(k) = 3 \cdot S(k - 1)$ for $k \ge 4$, and $S(3) = 3!$ because a hand of three cards cannot occur with only three cards.
solution: Only the relative order of the card numbers matters, so let $S(k)$ be the number of orderings of $k$ distinctly numbered cards on which the player does not lose. Call such orderings safe. The hand grows by at most one card per draw, so the player loses exactly when the hand ever holds at least $3$ cards. With $k = 3$ every ordering is safe. After at most two draws the hand holds at most $2$ cards, and after the third draw every card has been drawn, so all have been played and the hand is empty. Hence $S(3) = 6$. Now let $k \ge 4$ and let the smallest card, called card $1$, be in position $p$. If $p \ge 4$, then nothing can be played during the first three draws, so the hand holds $3$ cards and the player loses. So every safe ordering has $p \le 3$. Suppose $p \le 3$, and compare the game on the ordering with the reduced game on the same ordering with card $1$ deleted. Before card $1$ is drawn, the original game has at most $2$ cards drawn, so its hand holds at most $2$ cards. The first $p - 1$ draws of the reduced game likewise give a hand of at most $2$ cards. So neither game can be lost during these draws. For $t \ge p$, let $D$ be the set of the first $t$ cards drawn, which contains card $1$. After the rule is applied, the played cards are exactly the longest initial run of the card numbers contained in $D$, and the hand is the rest of $D$. The reduced game after $t - 1$ draws has drawn $D$ without card $1$. Its played cards are the same run without card $1$, so its hand is identical to the original hand. Thus the original game is lost at draw $t$ exactly when the reduced game is lost at draw $t - 1$, and these pairs cover all remaining draws of both games. Therefore an ordering with $p \le 3$ is safe exactly when its reduced ordering is safe. An ordering with $p \le 3$ corresponds bijectively to a choice of $p \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ together with an ordering of the other $k - 1$ cards. Hence $S(k) = 3 \cdot S(k - 1)$ for $k \ge 4$, which gives $S(7) = 3^4 \cdot 6 = 486$. The probability of not losing is $$\dfrac{486}{5040} = \dfrac{27}{280},$$ and $27$ and $280$ are coprime, since $27 = 3^3$ and $3$ does not divide $280$. Therefore $m + n = 27 + 280 = 307$. Why this works. recursion, bijection: once card $1$ is confined to three positions, deleting it matches safe orderings with safe orderings of one fewer card.
